slides.title: Complexification Adds Scalars
slides.notes: Open by framing complexification as a disciplined change of scalars, not as a license to forget the real problem. The chapter asks what a real object gains when complex coefficients are allowed. Emphasize that the same formulas continue to operate, but the set of allowable points, roots, and projective directions becomes larger and often easier to organize.

slides.title: Route Through The Chapter
slides.notes: Use this route slide to make the lecture feel like one construction repeated in several settings. First the vector space is complexified. Then maps and subspaces are checked for compatibility. After that, polynomial equations explain why complex points are useful. Finally affine and projective language keeps track of geometry whose coordinates may change while incidence and equations remain meaningful.

slides.title: Vector Space Complexification
slides.notes: Define the construction in the tensor-product form first, then immediately translate it into the concrete pair notation V plus iV. The point of the pair model is that students can see what i does: it swaps real and imaginary components with a sign. Stress that the real space is still present as the real slice, while the complexified space has twice the real dimension.

slides.title: Functoriality Extends Maps
slides.notes: Present functoriality as the safety rail for the whole chapter. If students complexify objects but forget how maps behave, the construction becomes ad hoc. The displayed rule says that the complexified map is determined componentwise. The identities for composition and identity maps mean that diagrams and algebraic dependencies from the real setting survive after changing scalars.

slides.title: Subspaces And Linear Equations
slides.notes: This slide is a good place to slow down and connect the abstract tensor product to computations. A vector lies in the complexified subspace exactly when both its real and imaginary parts satisfy the original subspace condition. If the subspace was defined by a matrix equation, the same matrix equation applies to complex vectors because matrix multiplication is polynomial in the entries.

slides.title: Polynomials Gain Complex Zeros
slides.notes: Use the roots-of-unity picture as the most concrete payoff of changing scalars. The equation has a real coefficient description, but the natural solution set lives around the complex unit circle. The computational certificate is not a proof of the algebraic theorem; it verifies that the generated visual is measuring the intended invariant, namely that these sample roots have modulus one.

slides.title: Real Directions Acquire Imaginary Companions
slides.notes: The notebook's first generated figure is deliberately simple because the conceptual move is subtle. The real line is still present as the baseline. The colored waves are not claiming that every complexified line is sinusoidal; they provide a visual proxy for independent imaginary displacement. Ask students to identify what is structural in the figure and what is merely a plotting convention.

slides.title: Affine Complexification
slides.notes: Move from vector spaces to affine spaces by emphasizing differences. Affine geometry does not have a distinguished zero vector, so one should not pretend that points are automatically vectors. Once a base point or chart is chosen, difference vectors live in the model vector space and can be complexified. Affine maps then extend because their linear parts extend functorially.

slides.title: Projective Complexification
slides.notes: Projective complexification is often where the change of scalars becomes geometrically vivid. The real projective line is not discarded; it becomes a real locus inside the complex projective object. The equivalence relation is broader because complex nonzero scalars are allowed. This is why a projective statement should be phrased using homogeneous equations, incidence, and ratios rather than a favorite coordinate representative.

slides.title: Coordinates Are Auxiliary
slides.notes: Use this slide as a conceptual guardrail before the final certificate. The chapter repeatedly warns against confusing a coordinate display with the object itself. In vector and affine settings, representatives depend on decomposition choices. In projective settings, many coordinate tuples represent the same point. The durable information is carried by equations, rank, incidence, and functorial behavior under maps.

slides.title: Computational Certificate
slides.notes: This certificate slide connects the lecture back to the notebook's computational contract. The purpose is not to replace proof with numerics. Instead, the checks verify that the produced figures are present, nonblank, and tied to the intended invariant. The root-modulus entry is especially useful because it turns a visual circle of red points into an auditable statement about the generated data.

slides.title: Recap And Board Questions
slides.notes: Close by returning to the chapter question: what does a real object gain when complex scalars are allowed? The answer is not just more coordinates. It gains a systematic companion category where maps, subspaces, equations, and projective incidence still behave coherently. The board questions are short checks that force students to practice the three central skills: extend a map, extend equations, and respect projective equivalence.
